episode_title: The New Emperor: Taira no Masakado and the Rebellion That Broke the Heian Court
youtube_title: The Samurai Who Declared Himself Emperor of Japan and Ruled for 60 Days
youtube_description:
In the winter of 939 a landholder on Japan's eastern frontier seized eight provinces, announced that a god had made him emperor, and set up a rival court against Kyoto. Sixty days later he was dead with an arrow in his forehead. His severed head is said to have flown home on its own — and the mound where it landed still sits between the skyscrapers of Tokyo's financial district, tended by the corporations that own the land around it. This is the story of Taira no Masakado.

teaser_narration: Shimosa plain, February 940. A man who calls himself the Emperor of Japan rides out with four hundred men against four thousand. Sixty days earlier he ruled eight provinces. What makes a samurai crown himself — and how did it end with a single arrow?
shorts_narration: Sixty days. That is how long Japan had two emperors. A warrior on the eastern plains crowned himself, seized eight provinces, and fell to one stray arrow. Taira no Masakado.

scenes.narration: In 939, a warrior declared himself emperor of Japan. He ruled eight provinces for sixty days, then lost his head. So why does Tokyo still keep a shrine to calm it?

scenes.narration: Taira no Masakado was born around the year 903 on the Bando plain — the eastern frontier of Japan, roughly three hundred miles from the capital, on the marshes and grasslands where Tokyo now stands. His grandfather had been born an imperial prince. The court, unable to support every descendant of Emperor Kanmu, had given him the surname Taira and sent him east to live off the land instead. Two generations later the family were not courtiers at all. They were horse-breeding landholders who settled their quarrels with bows, in a country the capital taxed but barely governed.

A few small figures of men in plain hemp working clothes moving between the buildings, tiny against the emptiness. Pale silver light, wide open sky, cold damp air. scenes.narration: As a young man Masakado went to Kyoto, as ambitious provincials did, and entered the service of Fujiwara no Tadahira, the most powerful man at court. He spent perhaps a decade there. What he wanted was a post in the imperial police — the office that would have made him, formally, a servant of the throne. He never got it. He was passed over for men with better connections, and around 931, after his father's death, he rode back east to claim his share of the family land. He came home with nothing from the capital but a patron's name.

scenes.narration: The east he came home to had no functioning law. His father's holdings had been carved up by his uncles while he was away, and in the provinces a land dispute was settled by whoever could put more mounted archers in a field. In the second month of 935 Masakado was ambushed at Nomoto, in Hitachi. He turned on his attackers, scattered them, and burned their settlements. Among the dead was his own uncle, Taira no Kunika. Kunika's son Sadamori was serving in Kyoto when the news reached him. He would spend the rest of his life on this.

scenes.narration: What followed was a private war lasting four years. His uncle Taira no Yoshikane burned villages, raised armies, and at one point carried painted images of Masakado's dead father and grandfather at the head of his troops, so that Masakado's men would have to shoot at their own ancestors. The archers hesitated. Masakado lost that engagement, and won nearly every other. Twice the court summoned him to Kyoto to answer for the killing. Twice he talked his way clear, once walking free under a general amnesty. In the east he was becoming something no provincial was supposed to be: untouchable.

Facing them across the grass, an opposing formation advances behind two tall poles carrying large painted silk portrait scrolls of solemn elderly Japanese noblemen in old-fashioned robes, held up like standards. Grey morning fog, muted colour, an unnatural stillness in the middle of a battle. All other banners are plain solid-colored fabric with no markings. scenes.narration: Men began bringing him their problems. Governors were sent out from Kyoto on four-year terms and treated their provinces as income; when one of them squeezed too hard, the injured party rode to Masakado. In 939 a landholder in Hitachi named Fujiwara no Haruaki, wanted by the governor for years of unpaid tax, fled to Masakado's estate and asked for protection. The governor demanded he be handed over. Masakado had sheltered fugitives before and argued his way clear each time. This time he did not argue. He gathered a thousand men and rode for the provincial capital.

scenes.narration: On the twenty-first day of the eleventh month of 939, Masakado's thousand met three thousand government troops outside the Hitachi provincial headquarters and broke them. His men burned the compound and emptied the storehouses, and the governor was taken prisoner. Then Masakado did the thing that could not be undone. He seized the provincial seal and the keys to the granaries — the physical instruments of imperial authority in the east. Until that morning he had been a violent man in a family quarrel. By that evening he was in rebellion against the Japanese state, and everyone involved understood it.

In the foreground, warriors in boxy early Heian o-yoroi armour carry out wooden chests and bales of rice while mounted men watch from the gate. Documents and lacquered boxes scattered in the mud. Ferocious orange firelight against deep blue night, heavy smoke, silhouetted figures. All banners plain solid-colored fabric with no markings. No text or written characters anywhere in the image.

scenes.narration: One of his companions — Okiyo, a minor prince who had been acting governor of Musashi until he fell out with his own deputy — put the situation to him plainly. The punishment for seizing one province, he said, and the punishment for seizing the whole of the Bando, are exactly the same. So take all of it. Masakado took the argument. Within weeks he had ridden into Shimotsuke and then Kozuke, and the governors handed over their seals and fled toward Kyoto rather than fight a man who had already burned one province down.

On the far bank a small group of terrified officials in court robes are loading ox-carts and fleeing along a road toward distant hills. Pale gold light low on the water, long shadows, immense scale. scenes.narration: By the first days of winter Masakado held Hitachi, Shimotsuke, Kozuke, Musashi, Sagami, Kazusa, Shimosa and Awa — the eight provinces of the Bando, the whole of the eastern plain. No warrior in the country's history had ever held so much. And it left him with an impossible problem. Every governor he had driven out was a lawful appointment of the throne. Every province he held, he held with no authority the court recognised. He commanded the east and, in law, did not exist. There were two ways out. Beg for pardon, or stop asking for it.

Thin columns of smoke rising at intervals across the whole horizon. A tiny formation of mounted men on the road, dwarfed by the land. scenes.narration: In the twelfth month of 939, at the provincial hall in Kozuke, a woman came forward and announced that she was a messenger of Hachiman, the god of war. The god, she said, was conferring the imperial title on Masakado, and the decree was endorsed by the spirit of Sugawara no Michizane — a scholar the court had exiled to his death, and whose vengeful ghost Kyoto genuinely feared. Masakado accepted. He took a title no subject in Japanese history had ever taken. Shinno. The New Emperor. For the first time, Japan had two.

Facing her, Taira no Masakado stands alone and upright — a powerfully built man in his mid thirties, broad weathered face, short black moustache and trimmed beard, in dark blue-laced armour over a russet robe, his expression caught between disbelief and acceptance. Smoke, torchlight raking across faces, deep black shadows in the rafters. Charged, ritual, ominous. No text or written characters anywhere in the image.

scenes.narration: He began building a state. He appointed his own governors to the eight provinces, named officials for a court, and chose a site in Shimosa for a capital and a palace. He even wrote to Fujiwara no Tadahira in Kyoto — his old patron — explaining himself, as though this were still a matter that could be discussed. Kyoto's answer was not a letter. The court held emergency rituals at every great temple, declared him a rebel, promised court rank to any man who killed him, and appointed a general to march east. The eastern warriors moved first.

Cold flat daylight, unfinished timber, an improvised throne room that looks temporary. No text or written characters anywhere in the image.

scenes.narration: In the second month of 940, Taira no Sadamori — the cousin whose father had died in Masakado's fires — joined Fujiwara no Hidesato, a hard-eyed officer from Shimotsuke, and raised four thousand men. Masakado had sent most of his army home for the planting season. He met them with about four hundred. The wind was at his back and he broke their first line. Then the wind turned into his face, and his arrows fell short, and their arrows did not. One struck him in the forehead. On the fourteenth day, the New Emperor was dead.

scenes.narration: He had held the title for barely two months. His head was carried to Kyoto and hung on a post beside the eastern market — the first time in recorded Japanese history that a warrior's head was displayed in the capital. His brothers were hunted down. Okiyo was killed. The rebellion in the west under Fujiwara no Sumitomo, which had terrified the court at the same moment, was crushed the following year. Sadamori and Hidesato received the rank and offices they had been promised, and Sadamori's descendants would one day rule Japan under a name everyone knows: the Taira.

A silent crowd of townspeople in plain robes and a few court officials in tall black caps stand back from it in a wide half circle. Bare willow trees, packed earth road, white plaster walls. Overcast light, muted colour, cold public dread. No text or written characters anywhere in the image.

scenes.narration: And then the story stopped being history. The head, people said, would not decay. Its eyes stayed open. It ground its teeth and called out for its body, and one night it lifted off the post and flew east, back toward the plain it came from. Where it fell, the villagers of Shibasaki buried it and raised a mound over it. That village is now Otemachi, the financial district of Tokyo. The mound is still there — a few square metres of shaded stone between the towers, on some of the most expensive ground on earth.

Silhouetted reeds and bare trees along the bottom of the frame, a scatter of tiny thatched roofs. Deep indigo sky, drifting cloud, cold moonlight on water. scenes.narration: Strip away the flying head and what remains is still remarkable. In sixty days a provincial landholder had taken eight provinces with private cavalry, and the imperial state — which had abandoned mass conscription a century and a half earlier — found it could not answer him with an army of its own. It had to hire other warriors and pay them in rank, office and land. That transaction is where the samurai begin as a political class. The court won in 940. But it won by handing its defenders exactly the power Masakado had seized.

The gap of empty floor between the two groups is the centre of the composition. Reed blinds, painted screen panels with landscape imagery only, cold north light from an open verandah. Restrained, formal, quietly historic. No text or written characters anywhere in the image.

scenes.narration: The mound in Otemachi has never been moved, and the reason is a long list of accidents. After the great earthquake of 1923 the Finance Ministry put temporary offices over the site. Within a few years the minister and a string of officials were dead, and the ministry rebuilt the mound and apologised to it. After the war, an occupation bulldozer that began work on the plot is said to have overturned and killed its driver. The corporations that own the surrounding towers still pay for the site's upkeep and attend its rites.

scenes.narration: Officially, Masakado was a traitor. In the east he was never anything of the kind. He was the man who had stood up to the capital's tax collectors, and he was worshipped for it — enshrined as a god at Kanda Myojin, one of Tokyo's great shrines, protector of the city's merchants and craftsmen. In 1874 the new Meiji government, rebuilding the nation around the emperor, struck him from the shrine's list of deities on the grounds that he was a rebel against the throne. He was not restored to it until 1984.

scenes.narration: What is strange about Masakado is how little ideology there is in him. He did not set out to overthrow anything. He fought his uncles over fields, sheltered a man the governor wanted, and discovered at every step that the only way out of the last fight was a bigger one — until the only title that fitted what he actually held was emperor. He took it, and it killed him in sixty days. A thousand years later, the country that condemned him still leaves flowers at his head, in the middle of its richest street.

scenes.narration: Next time on Samurai Chronicles: six and a half centuries later, a general so ill he could no longer see or sit a horse was carried onto the field at Sekigahara in a covered palanquin, his face wrapped in white cloth. He knew his friend's cause was hopeless. He had said so, to his friend's face. He fought for it anyway, held his flank as the betrayals broke around him, and died there by his own hand. Otani Yoshitsugu.
